Wald Test of Linear Constraints on Model Parameters

Source: R/wald_test.R
wald_test.Rd

Tests a set of linear equality constraints on the estimated parameters of a fitted model – for example, that a growth-factor mean is the same in three classes – without refitting the model under the constraints. The constraints name parameters by label; the labels are those of growth_estimates() for a growth model and those of vcov() for a covariate model (see Details).

Usage

wald_test(fit, constraints, rhs = 0, se = c("robust", "hessian", "opg"))

Arguments

fit

A model from fit_gmm() or fit_lcga(), or a mixture_model with a covariate structural model.

constraints

A list or matrix of constraints. See Details.

rhs

Numeric, the right-hand side \(r\): one value per constraint, or a single value recycled. Default 0.

se

For growth models, which covariance estimator to use: "robust" (default), "hessian" or "opg", as in growth_estimates(). Ignored for covariate models, whose covariance is the one the model was fitted with (see vcov()).

Value

A one-row data frame of class mixture_wald with columns Wald_Chi2, df, p_value and Method, the name of the covariance estimator behind the statistic.

Details

Writing the constraints as \(R\theta = r\), the statistic is $$W = (R\hat\theta - r)^\top (R \hat V R^\top)^{-1} (R\hat\theta - r),$$ referred to a chi-squared distribution with as many degrees of freedom as there are constraints (Wald, 1943). \(\hat V\) is the estimated covariance matrix of the parameters.

Labels. For a fit_gmm() or fit_lcga() fit, every row of growth_estimates(fit) is one parameter, labelled "<parameter>[<item>, <class>]": "growth_mean[intercept, 1]", "growth_variance[linear, 2]", "residual_variance[t1, 1]", and so on. A parameter constrained equal across classes appears once per class with the same value, and equating two of its copies is not a constraint at all. For a mixture model with a covariate structural model the labels are the names of vcov(fit), "Class k:predictor", which are the multinomial-logit coefficients relative to the class reported in its ref_class attribute.

Constraints. Either a list, each element one constraint:

  • a pair of labels, c("a", "b"), meaning a - b = 0;

  • a named numeric vector of weights, c(a = 1, b = -2), meaning a - 2 b = rhs;

or a numeric matrix with one row per constraint whose column names are labels. Three classes are equal on a parameter when two pairwise equalities hold, so list(c("a1", "a2"), c("a2", "a3")) has 2 degrees of freedom; a third equality, c("a1", "a3"), would add nothing and is refused as redundant.

Which test to use. wald_test() answers "are these parameters equal (or equal to these values)?" for any parameters of the model. analytical_wald_test() answers the narrower and common question "does this covariate affect class membership at all?", and needs only the covariate's name; on a covariate model it is the same statistic as wald_test() with every one of that covariate's coefficients set to zero. wald_omnibus_test() answers the same question from bootstrapped standard errors, for samples too small to trust the analytical ones.

Like any Wald test, this one assumes the estimates are near-normal, which fails near the edge of the parameter space: a variance close to zero, or a class with very few cases. A likelihood-ratio test of the constrained model against the free one settles those cases.

References

Wald, A. (1943). Tests of statistical hypotheses concerning several parameters when the number of observations is large. Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, 54(3), 426-482. doi:10.1090/S0002-9947-1943-0012401-3

See also

growth_estimates() for the labels and estimates of a growth model, analytical_wald_test(), wald_omnibus_test().

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n <- 400
cls <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
icept <- ifelse(cls == 1, 3, 1) + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
slope <- ifelse(cls == 1, 1.0, 0.2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)
y <- outer(icept, rep(1, 4)) + outer(slope, 0:3) + matrix(rnorm(n * 4, 0, 0.7), n, 4)
fit <- fit_gmm(y, times = 4, n_classes = 2, n_init = 10, random_state = 1)
# Do the two classes share their mean slope?
wald_test(fit, list(c("growth_mean[linear, 1]", "growth_mean[linear, 2]")))
#> =========================================================
#>                 WALD TEST (CONSTRAINTS)                  
#> =========================================================
#>   Method    : Sandwich (robust)
#> ---------------------------------------------------------
#>   Wald χ²(1) = 109.370,  p < .001
#> =========================================================
# }
